en: The *Nālandādahana*, a *ḍima* drama composed by Śrī Subrahmaṇya, characterized by the sentiments of heroism (*vīra*), wrath (*raudra*), terror (*bhayānaka*), and pathos (*karuṇa*).
It shines through the predominance of rasa (aesthetic flavor). This complete drama is performed at the great gate of Nālandā University.
[The opening verses include] the *nāndī*, Durgā, and so forth.
O you with eyes like blue lotuses, whose inner being is rippled with compassion;
O you of incomparable beauty, whose face has conquered the moon;
O you who reveal the further shore of the ocean of existence, O supreme yogi who brings about ultimate liberation.
O Hero who shatters the fortress of cruel misfortune,
O Conqueror of Māra, O Revealer of the Eightfold Path, O Renowned One, O Restrainer of the rutting elephant, O Most Excellent of Teachers, O Adored One!
Establisher of the prosperity of the land of Bhārata, abode of sacred virtues,
saluted by gods and men, wearer of the garland of hymns to Subrahmaṇya.
First Vision.
At the royal gate of the world-renowned Nālandā Mahāvihāra, some students were singing of its power;
then the presiding monk of the monastery and several senior monks arrived there and deliberated on means to repel the impending invasion by the Turuṣka army, while the students continued to sing.

We pay homage to our mother, Pūrvakalyāṇī, who is enriched with all auspicious qualities from beginning to end, renowned throughout all the worlds, and the noble lady of Nālandā; [those] from distant lands such as Kāmbhoja, Jagāndhāra, and Cīna have come here.
With our curiosity reflected [in this place], we have come from a distant land to the gateway of the ocean of all scriptures, which is adorned with arches; here,
these scholars have been equally examined by the guardians in various branches of learning.
Awakened by the direct perception of Nāgārjuna, who resembles an elephant that wards off logic-choppers,
they fill the earth with the light of knowledge and illuminate their mother, Nālandā, with the truths of the Buddha.
With full hearts, we pay homage to this foremost seat of learning in the three worlds.
We pay homage to the Mother of Nālandā, whose fame pervades all the worlds like the wind;
we pay homage to her who illuminates knowledge endowed with auspicious, truthful, and excellent qualities,
and who bestows both conventional and ultimate wisdom that removes the suffering of existence.
Then, the superintendent monk and his senior companions who had arrived there did not perceive the approaching power of the Turuṣka army.
The senior monk— 10.
I hear, I hear the sound of the Ābhīras and others approaching with great haste, like a flock of goats leaping over obstacles;
they are driven by greed toward Āryāvarta, the abode of wealth and storehouse of grain.
"Some say they are heroes," others say "they are exceedingly cruel," and still others say "they delight in terrible, great sins"; thus, having come from afar, they describe them with fear.
The Superintendent Bhikṣu, pacifying them, gives this reply.
"Enough of this 'asāverī' and so forth! Friend, calm your wandering mind; calm it!
Enough of this exaggeration regarding the news. In the inner apartments, there is a black cobra mistaken for a rat."
The beloved bellows, and you likewise prattle;
from such a proclamation, what fruit is there? It is as if the end of the eon has arrived.
The barbarians of Kaniṣka and Miṇḍha have acted like Buddhists.
Then, constantly recollecting how the arts and scriptures were composed in the past through faith by Śrīkara, Ārya, and Satya, [he realized that] even Mlecchas can always be brought under control.
Another elder monk said:
"Even though the Sahā world and so forth are burning, there are among them those who are learned in the treatises."
The learned ones sing of the power of those who have reached the further shore of the sciences of calculation and so forth, as well as of the *khaya*, *yāma*, *māla*,
and *barūṇi*; we, however, know [only] that which is based on the letters, places, and times.

We shall determine the eligibility of those seeking knowledge; for no one is capable of destroying Nalanda, which possesses a mother of complete and peerless learning at its gateway and whose fame is spread throughout the three worlds.
Then the first senior monk gave a severe reply:
"O fools! You who are devoid of knowledge of the true nature of the Mlecchas are speaking in vain."
O cruel one, even though you have recognized that their deeds are slightly terrifying,
you nevertheless entertain a desire to know about those most cruel enemies who destroy thousands of crafts and cause hundreds of temples to fall into ruin.
While others were distressed by the severing of their heads with swords— having dedicated their minds to the sacrifice of pulverizing the enemy host according to their own imagined scriptures—
a certain bhikkhunī, the superintendent of the library, proclaimed:
O Paṇḍita Tilaka and others, what is the fruit of speaking at length about the qualities of the Mlecchas?
If we desire to protect our mother according to our own will and according to our ability—
Without discussion, let us become warriors this very moment with haste;
though we are currently unarmed, without an army, and weak,
we shall remain steadfast in the preservation of our knowledge.
Let the Kirātas come; let us strive to pacify them.
Our effort would be in vain if we were to meet our death right here.
(Second Scene)
The ocean-like army of the Turuṣkas, having reached Nālandā with devotion toward their rival Jina, suddenly entered the royal gate;
mounting their horses and hacking at the disciples and monks with swords, they moved swiftly here and there.
In various places, they begin to burn those who are not their disciples.
One elder monk describes these terrible rites:
"In the sound of a swan, one [should recite] four times."

The Turuṣkas have arrived with extreme speed, like the wind, intent on crushing their enemies. (Verse 1) Wielding swords, they are devoted to the destruction of foes, skilled in breaking them, and intent on terrible deeds.
(Verse 2) Numbering in the thousands, they protect their own kin and are firm in their vow to strike down those who have come against them.
3. Mounted on horses, playing at the game of "piling up enemies," and deluded by greed for the wealth of others; 4.
Filling the sky with shouts of "Kill! Seize! Cut! and proclaiming their own arrival with many thousands of cries of "Harbīhattī."
Having seen all this shattered, the superintendent monk, his heart broken, lamented:
"O enemy of Mura!
Even though I saw your head already severed, I remained with my own head unsevered; now, sever my head!"
A0: Even upon seeing the groves unburnt by fire, I remained with my body unscathed; "Let my body burn!
[I cried]. C0: Alas! The courtyard of the four quarters is strewn with the corpses of a hundred slain mendicants;
indeed, the entire sky of Nalada is filled with blue-clad [monks].
Seeing the group of disciples fleeing here and there,
she did not know how she might save them, nor did she know how they might not.
Then, seeing the general beginning to burn the library, the bhikkhunī who was the librarian entreated him.
O Bhāgeśvarī,
first protect me, O high-minded one, sovereign of the great army! Protect me, O you who possess a treasury of accumulated knowledge consisting of hundreds of thousands of learned [teachings]!

And indeed, in this world where the human lifespan is so short, only a very brief practice is appropriate; nevertheless, through millions upon millions of efforts, the rivers of knowledge flow toward the ocean of wisdom.
Through those offered [to you], she who brings welfare to all shall flourish.
O Paṇḍita, from your country they will subject you to refutation; your treasury of scriptures is but a fabrication made by the fire-seller.
The general said:
"They are from Kuntala and Rāḍha; they are not opposed to the scriptures, and they subsist on food dear to Agni."
Furthermore, the scholars of the Qur'anic school say that [such efforts] are known to be fruitless; therefore, those who offer oblations to the fire are [futile].
The general, the friend, and the scholar of Arab eloquence pray thus.
"Husaini and others,
listen, O leader of the army! Listen with compassion to my beneficial words,
which have been spoken again and again by the Blessed One as the knowledge of the ultimate truth."
"Even in a foreign land, it must be sought and served"—
protect this world-renowned library from that fire!
Thus cries the commander-in-chief, overcome with anger.
"How can you subdue the fire of passion that has no refuge from the beginning?
O you who have cast away pride, I consider you a wise man indeed. Thus he spoke.
"Let the heads of the Turuṣka warriors be severed!

Let Nālandā, filled with its inhabitants, be consumed by fire by those roaming in all directions!"—saying this, he cut off the head of his own chief scholar. Then the army heroes, mounted on horses and moving swiftly in all directions, performed the severing of necks with swords and the burning of the city with fire with supreme enthusiasm. The nun who was the superintendent of the library entered the fire, while the superintendent monk, remaining profoundly peaceful, proclaimed a curse.
O Lion-King, in the midst of the assembly of fools— the Śrutimūḍhas, Atimūḍhas, Mlecchas, Cyutas, and Rākṣasas—
I proclaim the immediate destruction of the kingdom of the Musalmans as they approach.
Furthermore, the terrifying Mongol warriors, with their most fearsome roars,
bring to ruin all lands such as Śrīkaṇṭha, Musala, and Mālava, as well as the Persians and others, while loosening thousands of golden coins.
Devoid of compassion, you slay millions of people with swords and spears;
thus indeed your empire truly goes to destruction.
The truths of the Buddha-deity shine forth eternally;
like those intoxicated, the nun who is the librarian dances and proclaims them.

Nālandā, resounding with the continuous cries of birds and adorned by ten million disciples endowed with hundreds of beautiful virtues, is proclaimed as Yaśomatī— the Mother who bestows the sound of awakening like the moon.
O Mother Nālandā, born from the ocean of knowledge, whose stainless fame was not scorched even by millions of Turuṣka armies, you shine forth; victory, victory to you, O Indirā!
